accepted_prompt: Deleting an operator must never automatically delete the customer's Brain. If the Brain's subject asks to be deleted, erase that subject's Brain. If a Mindmake operator is removed, remove their access and require an explicit transfer or closure decision without deleting the subject's Brain.

subject_erasure.rule: A subject-erasure request may destroy only Brain data whose subject_id is the erased person.

operator_removal.rule: Removing an owner or operator revokes that person's access but must never use ownership alone as authority to delete another subject's Brain.

owned_customer_brain.rule: If the removed operator owns a workspace for a different subject, destructive account deletion stays held until an authorised successor accepts transfer or the customer explicitly authorises closure.

dual_role.rule: When the same person is both a Brain subject and an operator for other subjects, their own Brain may follow subject erasure while every other subject's Brain remains protected behind transfer or explicit closure.

decision_record.title: Brain subject and operator deletion separation
decision_record.decision: CTRL will erase a Brain only from verified subject authority, while removing an owner or operator will revoke access and require explicit transfer or customer-authorised closure without automatically deleting another subject's Brain.
rationale: The person a Brain describes and the person operating it can be different people.
An operator account lifecycle must not become accidental authority to destroy a customer's personal Brain.
Immediate access revocation contains access risk while explicit transfer or closure preserves customer control.
The same person can be a subject in one workspace and an operator in another, so deletion must be scoped by relationship rather than user identity alone.

alternatives.route: Cascade-delete every workspace owned by a removed user
alternatives.why_rejected: Ownership may represent Mindmake operations rather than the customer subject, so the cascade could destroy another person's Brain.

alternatives.route: Keep operator access until ownership transfer finishes
alternatives.why_rejected: It leaves unnecessary access open after removal and conflicts with the approved access-first containment rule.
The system must not invent authority over private customer Brain data.

decision_record.dissent: Transfer or closure can delay deletion of the operator's authentication identity and requires a safe custody state. This operational burden is accepted to prevent cross-subject destruction.
decision_record.tradeoffs: Operator removal may remain resumable pending until every differently-subjected workspace has an authorised transfer or explicit customer closure decision. CTRL accepts slower completion rather than silently deleting or reassigning a customer's Brain.

assumptions.assumption: Every Brain workspace can identify its actual subject independently from its current owner or operator.
assumptions.flip_rule: Reopen the planner boundary if a live workspace cannot establish one authoritative subject_id.

assumptions.assumption: A transfer or customer-authorised closure can be represented without restoring removed operator access.
assumptions.flip_rule: Reopen the custody mechanism if verified implementation evidence shows transfer requires restoring access to the removed operator.

revisit.trigger: A live workspace cannot establish its subject independently from its operator, transfer requires restoring removed access, or legal review requires a different custody or closure mechanism.
revisit.signal_source: Schema readback, multi-identity deletion canary, transfer recovery test or documented legal review
revisit.action_when_fired: Set this decision to review_due and prepare a bounded keep, supersede or reverse decision while preserving the no-cross-subject-deletion invariant.
